# Lusa v2.3.0 — safe, interrupt-driven UART, SPI, and I2C drivers

## Impact Introduction

v2.2.0 let Lusa firmware react to hardware interrupts, but every program still
had to program raw registers, invent its own buffering, and trust that no other
code touched the same peripheral. That is where most bare-metal bugs live:
two parts of a program driving one UART, a byte lost because the main loop was
busy, or a race between a handler and the code that reads its buffer.

v2.3.0 ships a driver layer that removes that work:

- A bundled crate, `lusa::hal`, provides `uart`, `spi`, and `i2c` drivers with
  one API on STM32F4, RP2040, ESP32-C3, and the host. `use lusa::hal::uart;`
  is all a program needs; the build target picks the register-level backend.
- Drivers are interrupt-driven and buffered. Writes queue bytes in a ring and
  return immediately; the interrupt handler feeds the transmitter and fills the
  receive ring. The main program never polls a status register.
- Hardware blocks have exactly one owner. `take()` hands out a peripheral
  token once, and the new `#[peripheral]` attribute makes that token move-only
  in the interpreter, the bytecode VM, and the C11 checker, so it cannot be
  copied or cloned into a second owner.
- Renode now emulates the whole path on all three boards: an SPI loopback, an
  I2C echo device, and repository models for the blocks Renode 1.17 lacks.

Existing programs are unchanged; nothing is added to a program that does not
mention `lusa::`.

## Feature Highlights

- **`#[peripheral]` resource tokens:** a `#[peripheral]` struct moves on
  assignment, by-value calls, and `return` even with scalar fields; reuse is
  `E1001`, and `clone` of the token or of any struct containing it is the new
  `E1006`. Driver calls take the token by `borrow`.
- **Single claims:** `uart::take()`, `spi::take()`, and `i2c::take()` return
  `Some(token)` the first time and `None` afterwards.
- **Ring buffers with critical sections:** each driver owns a 64-byte receive
  ring and a 64-byte transmit ring. Every ring operation runs inside
  `interrupts_disable`/`interrupts_restore`, which also acts as a compiler
  barrier. `write`/`transfer`/`queue` return `false` instead of blocking when a
  ring is full, and `overruns` counts received bytes dropped on a full ring.
- **UART:** `configure(port, baud)`, `write`, `read` (`Option<u32>`),
  `available`, `pending`, `is_busy`, `flush`, `idle`, `on_interrupt()`.
  STM32F4 USART2, RP2040 PL011 UART0, ESP32-C3 UART0.
- **SPI:** `configure(bus, frequency_hz, mode)` with modes 0-3 and the closest
  divider, full-duplex `transfer`, `read`, `flush`. STM32F4 SPI1, RP2040 PL022
  SPI0, ESP32-C3 GP-SPI2.
- **I2C:** `queue` plus `start_write(bus, address)`,
  `start_read(bus, address, count)`, and `wait` returning 0 (done), 1 (NACK),
  or 2 (bus error). STM32F4 I2C1 event/error state machine, RP2040
  DesignWare command FIFO, ESP32-C3 command list.
- **Board bring-up included:** `configure` enables the block's clock, releases
  its reset, routes its pins, and unmasks its interrupt. New vectors:
  STM32F4 `i2c1_ev` (47), `i2c1_er` (48), `spi1` (51); RP2040 `spi0` (34),
  `i2c0` (39). On ESP32-C3 the drivers route UART0, SPI2, and I2C through the
  interrupt matrix to CPU interrupt 11, so one
  `#[interrupt("machine_external")]` handler serves all three.
- **Host simulation:** on the host the drivers are software models, so driver
  code runs under `lusalang run` and `--vm`. `uart::sim_receive`/`sim_sent`,
  `spi::sim_reply_offset`, and `i2c::sim_attach` play the other end of the
  wire.
- **Stable diagnostics:** the crate is spliced onto line 1 (after
  `#[no_std]`), so errors in your program keep their line numbers, and the CLI
  now renders diagnostics against the expanded program. `lusa::` works as a
  path root from any module.
- **Renode platforms:** each board gains an SPI loopback (MISO wired to MOSI)
  and an `EchoI2CDevice` at `0x55`. `renode/models/` adds C# models for the
  RP2040 PL022 and the ESP32-C3 UART, GP-SPI2, and I2C controller, loaded by
  the new `@MODELS@` monitor-script line. The RISC-V platforms now declare
  Zicsr CPUs to match the compiler flags.
- **Runnable example:** `examples/interrupt_uart_echo.lusa` is an STM32F4 echo
  server that echoes every byte and reports the length of each line.
- **Hardware tests:** `tests/module27_drivers.rs` covers the attribute, move
  and clone rules in every engine, crate resolution and line numbers, the host
  models, vectors and platforms, cross builds, and Renode runs of the echo
  server plus an SPI/I2C/ownership check on STM32F4, RP2040, and ESP32-C3.
- **Fixes:** native `and`/`or` expressions and literal constant folding
  (`4 + 256`) no longer fail with `E1001` inside the self-hosted compiler; the
  bytecode VM now enforces move semantics for heap-bearing structs like the
  interpreter; and `#s`, `string.byte`, and `string.sub` are constant-time on
  ASCII strings, which made native builds of large programs up to 8x faster.

## How to Use

The host drivers run anywhere the release binary runs:

```lusa
use lusa::hal::uart
use lusa::hal::i2c

-- A peer types "hi" into the simulated serial port.
local port = uart::take():unwrap()
uart::configure(borrow port, 115200)
print("second claim:", uart::take())
uart::sim_receive(104)
uart::sim_receive(105)

-- Echo every byte; `idle` delivers the simulated interrupt.
local echoed = 0
while echoed < 2 do
    match uart::read(borrow port) with
    | Some(byte) =>
        uart::write(borrow port, byte)
        echoed = echoed + 1
    | None => uart::idle(borrow port)
    end
end
uart::flush(borrow port)
local line = ""
local more = true
while more do
    match uart::sim_sent() with
    | Some(byte) => line = line .. string.char(byte)
    | None => more = false
    end
end
print("echoed:", line)

-- I2C: write two bytes to the modelled device at 0x55, read them back.
local bus = i2c::take():unwrap()
i2c::configure(borrow bus, 100000)
i2c::queue(borrow bus, 7)
i2c::queue(borrow bus, 9)
i2c::start_write(borrow bus, 85)
print("write status:", i2c::wait(borrow bus))
i2c::start_read(borrow bus, 85, 2)
print("read status:", i2c::wait(borrow bus), i2c::read(borrow bus):unwrap(), i2c::read(borrow bus):unwrap())
i2c::queue(borrow bus, 1)
i2c::start_write(borrow bus, 34)
print("nobody at 0x22:", i2c::wait(borrow bus))
```

```sh
lusalang run hal_demo.lusa
lusalang run hal_demo.lusa --vm
```

Output:

```text
second claim: None
echoed: hi
write status: 0
read status: 0 7 9
nobody at 0x22: 1
```

On a board, the same API is driven by the hardware interrupt:

```lusa
#[no_std]
use lusa::hal::uart;

#[interrupt("USART2")]
function serial_irq(): void
    uart::on_interrupt()
end

#[entry]
function main(): void
    local port: uart::Uart = uart::take():unwrap()
    uart::configure(borrow port, 115200)
    interrupts_enable()
    while true do
        match uart::read(borrow port) with
        | Some(byte) => uart::write(borrow port, byte)
        | None => uart::idle(borrow port)
        end
    end
end
```

```sh
lusalang build examples/interrupt_uart_echo.lusa --target stm32f4
cargo test --test module27_drivers -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture
```

Use `#[interrupt("UART0")]` on RP2040 and `#[interrupt("machine_external")]`
on ESP32-C3. With `LUSA_ARM_CC`, `LUSA_ESP32_CC`, and `LUSA_RENODE` set, the
module 27 suite types `hello lusa`, `ping`, and `!` into each board's UART and
expects:

```text
LUSA ECHO READY
hello lusa
[ 10 bytes]
ping
[ 4 bytes]
bye l=2
```

## Compatibility / Limits

- v2.2.0 and earlier releases are unchanged, and programs that do not mention
  `lusa::` compile exactly as before.
- Native programs that use `lusa::hal` must be `#[no_std]`: driver state lives
  in promoted module globals. `riscv32-virt` and `riscv64-virt` ship no drivers
  and report `lusa::hal has no drivers for target ...`.
- One instance per block (STM32F4 USART2/SPI1/I2C1, RP2040 UART0/SPI0/I2C0,
  ESP32-C3 UART0/SPI2/I2C), 8-bit SPI frames, and 7-bit I2C addresses. DMA,
  chip-select control, interrupt priorities, and 10-bit addressing are left to
  the application.
- The drivers assume the reset clock tree: STM32F4 16 MHz HSI, RP2040 125 MHz
  `clk_sys` feeding `clk_peri`, ESP32-C3 80 MHz APB. One I2C transaction reads
  at most 16 bytes on RP2040 and moves at most 31 written / 32 read bytes on
  ESP32-C3.
- The RP2040 PL022 and the ESP32-C3 controllers run in Renode against
  repository models written from the reference manuals; they cover the
  registers the drivers use. Renode's DesignWare I2C model does not report
  address NACKs, so the RP2040 NACK path is verified on hardware only.
- Diagnostics show the expanded program line, where module paths appear under
  their internal `__lusa_m_...` names.
- Lusa still has no bitwise binary operators; the drivers update register
  fields with arithmetic.

## Installation

Download `lusa-setup.zip` for Windows, or the matching
`lusa-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `lusa-linux-arm64.tar.gz`, or
`lusa-macos-arm64.tar.gz` archive. Unpack it and run `lusalang version` to
confirm `2.3.0`.

The release archives contain the host `lusalang` binary, which includes the
`lusa::hal` crate. To build firmware, install `arm-none-eabi-gcc` or a GNU
RISC-V compiler separately and set `LUSA_ARM_CC` / `LUSA_ESP32_CC`, or put the
compiler on `PATH`. Install Renode separately to run the images; the
repository's `renode/` directory holds the platforms, scripts, and peripheral
models.
